Chapter 7: The Rumble—Challenging the First Draft.
So, after facing the reckoning, comes what we call the rumble. It’s that moment when you dig a little deeper into the stories you tell yourself—those quick judgments and assumptions your mind rushes to fill in. Most of us don’t even notice how fast our brains leap to conclusions, patching together gaps with old hurts and familiar beliefs. But here’s the thing: that first draft of any story in your mind? It’s almost never the full truth.
Picture this. There’s a project manager who finds herself left out of an important meeting. Instantly, she feels sidelined. Her thoughts race back to old memories of being excluded, and that sting of rejection comes rushing in. But instead of reacting straight away, she pauses and wonders, “Wait... what else might be true here? Is there another reason this happened?”
That’s the heart of the rumble. It’s not about accepting that first emotional draft—it’s about getting curious, asking yourself questions, and really exploring the feelings that are driving your story. For example, think about a father who just had a tough exchange with his daughter. His mind starts spinning tales about being a bad parent. But when he stops and checks in with himself, he realizes that under all that frustration... there’s actually fear—fear of losing connection, fear of not being good enough.
Most of us don’t realize how much our stories are shaped by our old wounds and unspoken fears. The rumble gives us a chance to shine a light on those patterns, to question them, and maybe even rewrite how the story goes. Imagine a friend who’s just had a falling out. She’s convinced she’s always the one left behind. But when she looks closer, she sees echoes of her own childhood shaping how she reacts now. That awareness helps her find the courage to reach out, have a hard conversation, and start to heal.
Remember, rumbling isn’t about blaming yourself or anyone else. It’s about understanding—realizing that your first mental draft is just that: a draft. By slowing down and really looking at your own narrative, you give yourself the chance to respond with clarity and compassion, instead of just reacting out of habit.
Take the example of a coach who’s just lost a big game. His first reaction? Blame the referees, blame his players. But when he takes a moment to reflect, he recognizes something deeper—his own fear of letting down the team, and the weight of the pressure he’s been feeling. That insight doesn’t change the score, but it does change his perspective. He’s able to meet his players with empathy, not just frustration.
Here’s what’s powerful: rumbling with your stories is something you get better at with practice. Every time you hit a setback, you’ve got a new chance to pause, reflect, and ask yourself, “What story am I telling myself? What feelings are fueling this? And honestly, what else might be true?” Over time, this way of approaching challenges builds self-awareness, empathy, and a real ability to rise strong—even when things get tough.
